    AI Overview
    Navroz (Nowruz) is the Persian New Year celebrated by over 300 million people worldwide, marking the spring equinox (around March 21) as a time of renewal and rebirth. It is celebrated by Iranians, Kurds, Parsi Zoroastrians, and various ethnic groups across Central Asia, the Middle East, and the Balkans, including Afghanistan, Pakistan, Turkey, and Azerbaijan. 
    Key Groups and Regions Celebrating Navroz: 
    • Iranians: It is the most significant national holiday, marked by the setting of the Haft Sin table.
    • Parsi Zoroastrians
      :
      The Parsi community in India and Pakistan celebrates this as the start of their new year, visiting fire temples and wearing new clothes.
    • Kurds: A major national celebration that unites Kurds across Iraq, Syria, and Turkey.
    • Central Asia & Middle East: Widely observed in Afghanistan, Tajikistan, Uzbekistan, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, and Azerbaijan.
    • Other Communities: Celebrated by Azerbaijani, Turkish, Turkmen, and Uyghur communities. 
    Main Traditions of the Celebration: 
    • Haft-Seen Table: Iranians place seven symbolic items starting with the Persian letter 'S' to symbolize spring and renewal.
    • Spring Cleaning: Known as "dusting away the past," houses are cleaned to welcome the new year.
    • Fire Rituals: Bonfires are lit to symbolize light and warmth, triumphing over darkness.
    • Family Gatherings: Visiting relatives, particularly elders, and wearing new clothes.
    • Culinary Traditions: Special meals such as sabzi polo (herbed rice) and Haft Mewa (seven fruits) are prepared. 
    Recognized by UNESCO as part of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity, it is a secular celebration of nature's rebirth.

      AI Overview
      Nowruz foods symbolize renewal, abundance, and the arrival of spring, with iconic dishes including Sabzi Polo Mahi (herb rice with fish) for prosperity, Kuku Sabzi (herb frittata) for fertility, and Ash-e Reshteh (noodle soup) for a smooth journey, alongside sweets like Shirin Polo (sweet rice) and celebratory nuts and dried fruits for good fortune. These dishes feature fresh greens, rice, and symbolic ingredients like saffron, barberries, and nuts, varying regionally but centered on themes of new beginnings.
       
      Main Dishes
      • Sabzi Polo Mahi: A signature dish of herbed rice (parsley, dill, cilantro) served with pan-fried or baked fish, symbolizing life and abundance. 
      • Kuku Sabzi: A vibrant frittata packed with fresh herbs, eggs, and sometimes walnuts and barberries, representing fertility and happiness. 
      • Ash-e Reshteh: A thick soup with herbs, beans, and special noodles (reshteh), with the noodles symbolizing the winding paths of life. 
      • Reshteh Polo: Aromatic rice cooked with noodles, often served with chicken or lamb. 
      Sweets & Sides
      • Shirin Polo: A festive "sweet rice" with saffron, orange peel, pistachios, and almonds, bringing joy and sweetness. 
      • Zereshk Polo: Saffron rice studded with tart barberries, often served with chicken. 
      • Samanu: A sweet, creamy pudding made from sprouted wheat, found on the Haft-Seen table. 
      • Ajil-e Moshkel Gosha: A special mix of nuts and dried fruits for good fortune, eaten during gatherings. 
      Regional Variations & Symbolic Items
      • Azerbaijan: Features kebabs, dolma (stuffed vine leaves), and sweets like baklava and shekerbura.
      • Uzbekistan: Centerpiece is Plov, a rice dish with meat and vegetables, and Sumalak, a sweet wheat pudding. 
      • Afghanistan: Includes Sabzi Challow (spinach and lamb curry) and Kolcheh Nowrozi (rice flour biscuits). 
      • Haft-Seen Table: Includes symbolic items like Sabzeh (sprouted greens), Seeb (apple), Senjed (oleaster fruit), Samanu, Seer (garlic), Somāq (sumac), and Serkeh (vinegar).

        AI Overview
        Nowruz celebrates the spring equinox with deep-cleaning homes, setting up symbolic {Haft-Seen tables} (with items like sprouts, apples, vinegar, coins), jumping over bonfires (Chaharshanbe Suri), feasting on special foods (like Plov/Pilaf), exchanging gifts, and spending time in nature, especially on the 13th day (Sizdah Bedar), symbolizing renewal, life, and new beginnings across cultures from Iran to Central Asia.
         
        Key Traditions & Rituals
        • Khaneh Tekani (Spring Cleaning): Weeks before, families thoroughly clean homes to welcome the new year. 
        • Haft-Seen Table: A central display with seven symbolic items starting with the letter 'S' in Persian (e.g., Sabzeh for rebirth, Samanu for prosperity, Seeb for health) plus candles, eggs, and a mirror. 
        • Chaharshanbe Suri (Fire Festival): On the last Tuesday night, people light bonfires and jump over them, chanting "My yellow to you, my red to me," to exchange sickness for health. 
        • Food & Feasting: Special meals like Plov (rice with meat/vegetables), Ash-e Reshteh (noodle soup), sweets, and Sumanak (wheat pudding) are prepared and shared. 
        • Visiting & Gifting: Families visit each other, exchange gifts (especially for children), and share traditional sweets. 
        • Sizdah Bedar (Nature Day): On the 13th day, families picnic outdoors, symbolically discarding the Sabzeh (sprouts) into running water to cast away negativity. 
        Cultural Variations
        • Central Asia: Traditions include public feasts, nomadic games (wrestling, horse racing), and building yurts, with hearty soups like Nauryz Koje. 
        • UNESCO Recognition: Recognized globally as a day of peace and renewal, celebrated by diverse communities worldwide.

          AI Overview
          Nowruz originates from ancient Persia, with roots in Zoroastrianism over 3,000 years ago, celebrating the vernal equinox and the first day of spring as a symbol of rebirth, new beginnings, and the triumph of good over evil. It marks the Persian New Year, symbolizing renewal and harmony with nature, with legends tying it to mythical King Jamshid who brought light and prosperity back to the world after darkness. Recognized by UNESCO and the UN, it's celebrated across West Asia, the Caucasus, Central Asia, and South Asia with local variations.
           
          Historical Roots
          • Zoroastrianism: Nowruz was a significant feast day in ancient Persia, linked to the Zoroastrian faith, which saw the return of spring as spiritually important. 
          • Ancient Persia: Celebrated in ancient cities like Persepolis and mentioned in texts like the Shāh-nāmeh, it's deeply tied to Persian culture. 
          Mythological Origins
          • King Jamshid: A popular myth tells of King Jamshid creating a jeweled throne that flew, bringing light and joy to his people on the first day of spring, establishing the festival. 
          • Triumph of Good: It represents the defeat of darkness (Ahriman) by good (Jamshid), bringing prosperity and life. 
          Modern Significance
          • Renewal: A time for spring cleaning (khane tekani) and symbolic burning of negativity, welcoming fresh starts. 
          • Cultural Unity: Celebrated by diverse cultures and religions across vast regions, embodying shared heritage. 
          • International Recognition: The UN proclaimed March 21 as International Nowruz Day in 2010. 
          Key Traditions
          • Haft-Seen Table: A centerpiece in Iran with seven symbolic items starting with the letter 'S' (seen) representing new life. 
          • Festivities: Include family gatherings, special meals (like plov), music, dancing, and jumping over bonfires (Chaharshanbe Suri).
